competencies.name: Grounding and hallucination fixes
competencies.posting_quote: The agent sometimes says a product is unavailable when it's in stock.

competencies.name: Hybrid exact and semantic retrieval
competencies.posting_quote: We need both, in one ranking.

competencies.name: Multilingual quality
competencies.posting_quote: An agent that answers in the wrong language is worse than one that says nothing.

competencies.name: Latency and cost
competencies.posting_quote: You'll profile requests, test prompt and model changes, and ship improvements you can point at on a graph.

competencies.name: Evals that predict production
competencies.posting_quote: Making it actually predict production quality is open work.

competencies.name: Reading traces and debugging
competencies.posting_quote: Given a bad answer in production, you can find why: retrieval missed, the prompt was wrong, the model picked the wrong tool.

competencies.name: Scoring and suppressing proactive insights
competencies.posting_quote: Ranking, scoring, and suppressing proactive insights so the agent interrupts a customer only when it has earned it.

competencies.name: RAG fundamentals
competencies.posting_quote: You know how RAG actually behaves: embeddings, vector search, chunking, reranking, and where each one breaks.

evidence.text: Built a product-question assistant for a fashion webshop, with pgvector retrieval over 38,000 catalogue items and answers in Swedish and English.

evidence.text: Cut out-of-stock hallucinations from 9% to 2% with an exact SKU and size lookup before semantic search plus a grounding check on the final answer.

evidence.text: Reduced median answer latency from 4.1 s to 2.3 s by caching embeddings, trimming the prompt and streaming the first sentence.

questions.text: Thanks for joining. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself and what you have been building recently?
What draws you to Brightwave and to this AI Engineer role in particular?
follow_ups: What part of building proactive agents interests you most?
What would you want to have owned after your first few months?

questions.text: Imagine our agent tells a customer that a product is unavailable when it is actually in stock. How would you find out why, and how would you fix it?
follow_ups: What would you look at first in the trace?
How would you prove the fix worked and stays fixed?

questions.text: Semantic search handles a warm jacket for winter well but struggles with a SKU or a specific size. How would you combine exact and semantic matching in one ranking?
follow_ups: How would you decide how to weigh the two signals?
Where does a reranker fit, and where does it break down?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you worked on an assistant that had to answer in more than one language. What went wrong, and what did you do about it?
follow_ups: How did you measure quality in each language?
What would you do differently now?

questions.text: Tell me about a time you made an LLM feature faster or cheaper. How did you find the bottleneck?
follow_ups: What was the number before and after?
Did any change hurt answer quality, and how did you check?

questions.text: Our golden-dataset harness does not yet predict production quality well. How would you go about making it more predictive?
follow_ups: Where would new test cases come from?
How would you know the eval score and production quality actually agree?

questions.text: Suppose a proactive agent has ten possible things it could tell a customer right now. How would you decide which one, if any, is worth saying?
follow_ups: What signals would you use to score an insight?
How would you measure whether suppressing an insight was the right call?

c1.1: Blames the model in general and proposes a vague prompt tweak, with no way to locate or verify the cause.
c1.3: Separates retrieval, prompt and model causes and suggests a stock or grounding check, but gives little measurement.
c1.5: Traces the failing case, adds exact lookup and a grounding check against stock data, and shows the hallucination rate falling with numbers on a fixed test set.

c2.1: Treats semantic search as the only option and cannot explain why SKUs and sizes fail.
c2.3: Describes combining keyword or exact lookup with vector search, but is vague about how the results are merged.
c2.5: Explains how exact and semantic results are merged in one ranking, with weighting and reranking, and checks the result against recall on a golden set.

c3.1: Says the model handles any language and has no way to detect wrong-language answers.
c3.3: Knows multilingual prompts fail and describes language detection or per-language checks.
c3.5: Gives a concrete failure, enforces answer language, tests each language on its own set, and reports the improvement.

c4.1: Talks about speed in general terms with no measurement or numbers.
c4.3: Profiles requests and names sensible changes such as caching or shorter prompts, with partial numbers.
c4.5: Measures before and after on latency and cost, names the bottleneck, ships specific changes, and checks that quality did not drop.

c5.1: Relies on manual spot checks or a static test set with no link to production.
c5.3: Maintains a golden set and runs it before changes, but does not check whether scores match real outcomes.
c5.5: Grows the golden set from real production traces, validates eval scores against production quality, and runs the evals in CI to block regressions.

c6.1: Cannot say where to look for the cause of a bad answer.
c6.3: Reads a trace and sorts the failure into retrieval, prompt or tool choice.
c6.5: Walks through a trace step by step, isolates retrieval, prompt or tool selection as the cause, and turns the finding into a fix and a regression test.

c7.1: Suggests sending every possible insight or picks at random, with no notion of cost to the customer.
c7.3: Proposes scoring insights by relevance and setting a threshold, with limited thought on measurement.
c7.5: Designs a scoring and suppression approach with clear signals and an explicit cost of interrupting, and plans to measure suppressed versus sent insights.

c8.1: Only names RAG components and cannot say how or where they fail.
c8.3: Explains embeddings, chunking and reranking with some failure modes seen in practice.
c8.5: Explains where each RAG stage breaks with real examples from production, backed by measured results such as recall.
